Once the object's position relative to a spherical mirror is known, the **position of its image** can be determined by a ray diagram.
First construct the image of any point on the object, then use a straightedge and compass to determine the directions of the reflected rays.
The focusing constructions below use the paraxial approximation.

To construct the reflected ray for incident ray $AC$, first draw a secondary optical axis parallel to it (Figure 147).
This secondary axis intersects the mirror's focal plane at point $D$.
The line $CD$, from the point of incidence on the mirror through this intersection, is the required reflected path.

This construction is based on the following result: paraxial rays parallel to the same secondary optical axis converge after reflection at the same point in the focal plane (see Figure 144).
Only one of these rays needs to be considered to locate that point.
Choose the ray that passes through the mirror's center of curvature $O$ and coincides with the secondary axis.

After reflection, this ray retraces its original straight line, so its reflected path also passes through the unknown point $D$.
Thus, $D$ lies in both the focal plane and this secondary axis, at their intersection.
The following rays can be used to construct the image of any point $A$ on an object (Figure 148).
1. Ray $AOC$, which passes through the center of curvature, retraces its original straight line along reflected path $COA$.
2. Ray $AFK$, which passes through the mirror's focus, is reflected parallel to the principal axis.
3. Ray $AP$, which strikes the mirror's vertex, has a reflected ray symmetric to the incident ray about the principal axis.
4. Incident ray $AE$, which is parallel to the principal axis, has a reflected path $EFA_1$ through the focus.

In the paraxial imaging model described in the figure, all rays from $A$ that strike the mirror pass through image point $A_1$ after reflection.
To locate $A_1$, **any two** of the rays listed above are sufficient.
The other incident rays also pass through the same image point $A_1$ after reflection.

A real mirror may not reflect every selected type of ray.
For example, some concave medical mirrors have a small central hole and cannot reflect rays that strike the hole.
An image can still be constructed using rays reflected by the parts that have a reflecting surface.
To construct the image of the entire object, it is sufficient to construct the images of points along its **edges**.
